title: Office of Communication of the United Church of Christ v. FCC (1966)
shortTitle: Office of Communication of the United Church of Christ v. FCC (1966)
summary: Public-interest participants could obtain a licensing hearing to present allegations that a station had refused to air support for racial desegregation.
notes: The station was WLBT in Jackson, Mississippi, the opinion was written by then-Judge Warren Burger, and its core holding is that representatives of the listening public have standing as 'parties in interest' to intervene in license renewal proceedings; after the remand hearing the same court in 1969 (UCC II) ordered the license vacated.

sections.Parties: A local church and two civil-rights activists challenged the FCC’s handling of a Mississippi television station’s renewal application.
sections.Material Facts: The station was obligated to broadcast multiple points of view on significant public-policy questions. The petitioners alleged it had refused programming supporting racial desegregation. The governing statute required a hearing when the FCC could not make the necessary public-interest finding.
sections.Procedural History: The petitioners sought a formal hearing to present their allegations. The D.C. Circuit agreed that one was required.
sections.Issue: Could persons representing the listening public invoke the hearing process even though the adjudication directly concerned someone else’s broadcast license?
sections.Holding: The petitioners were entitled to a formal hearing in this public-interest licensing setting.
sections.Reasoning: The statutory public-interest responsibility made representation of affected listeners relevant to whether the FCC could make its required renewal finding. The editors treat this as a defined exception to the general rule against third parties demanding hearings on another person’s legal rights and connect it to participation as a source of administrative legitimacy.

topics.lrs-o-third-party-hearings: Public-interest representatives could invoke a renewal hearing where their allegations undermined the necessary public-interest finding.
topics.lrs-n-standing-apa702: The case established that members of the listening public are 'persons aggrieved' entitled to participate in and seek review of licensing decisions, a precursor to modern statutory-standing analysis.
